scope: Active manuscript citations only. Metadata and relevant methods/results/limitations passages read from actual PDFs; this is claim-focused verification, not a systematic review or a claim to exhaustive cover-to-cover reading.
recent_definition: First publication in calendar years 2024–2026; online publication takes precedence over issue year.

references.manuscript_sections: 1. Introduction; 2.1. Assistance timing and proactive coordination
references.supported_claim: Andriella et al. model assistance type, timing, and confidence [1] Andriella et al. learn proactive assistance from user profiles and task state in a sequential memory game, jointly addressing assistance type, timing, and confidence [1].
references.interpretation_limit: Supports the three decision dimensions and this particular game implementation. It does not establish a physiological trigger or validate the present HR-rise threshold.

references.version: Conference paper in university repository; PDF includes ResearchGate cover
references.supported_claim: Adjacent assembly work by Caiazzo et al. compares manual, collaborative, and guided collaborative conditions, with EEG used for workload assessment [2].
references.interpretation_limit: The N=3 qualification is essential. This is adjacent assembly evidence, not a test of our timing policy. Unverified DOI and proceedings pagination are omitted from the bibliography.

references.supported_claim: Capponi et al. similarly find no clear RMSSD pattern across their assembly configurations and distinguish cognitive effort from stress [3].
references.interpretation_limit: The negative RMSSD finding is specific to these tasks/configurations. It does not mean every cardiac measure is uninformative or that physiological state has no relationship with workload.

references.version: ICRA paper hosted by MERL, technical-report cover
references.manuscript_sections: 1. Introduction; 2.1. Assistance timing and proactive coordination; 6.3. Limitations and future work
references.supported_claim: PACE uses action-completion estimates to coordinate proactive assistance [4]. PACE also compares proactive assistance with an explicit-query condition in which participants press a button to request help; participant waiting times were longest under explicit query [4]. PACE estimates action completion from hand movements and uses a learned policy to coordinate assistance during collaborative assembly [4]. PACE found longer participant waiting times under explicit query than under proactive assistance [4]
references.interpretation_limit: This is hand-motion/task-progress assistance, not physiology-based assistance. PDF p. 1 is a MERL cover and p. 2 is blank; the actual article begins on PDF p. 3. Explicit query requests follow completion of each assembly action; it is not necessarily a request for a reasoning hint. No claim that requested help is universally less helpful or a significant query-versus-PACE waiting contrast is imported.

references.supported_claim: Hart describes the six NASA-TLX workload dimensions and the use of an unweighted overall score [5].
references.interpretation_limit: Hart supports describing and qualifying an adaptation; it does not validate our particular seven-point items, scoring, or psychometric properties. The paper is from 2006, regardless of its 2026 NASA upload path.

references.supported_claim: Hostettler et al. adapt robot behavior to user distance while measuring pupil responses; direct pupil-driven adaptation is a future direction [6].
references.interpretation_limit: Do not cite the paper as an implemented pupil-triggered assistance policy. Its table of possible human characteristics includes prior literature; that table alone is not evidence of what its own experiment implemented.

references.manuscript_sections: 1. Introduction; 2.1. Assistance timing and proactive coordination
references.supported_claim: A recent review distinguishes adaptation of robot motion from task-level decisions about timing, sequencing, and role allocation [7]. Karbouj et al.'s review of adaptive industrial HRC distinguishes motion, task, and control adaptations and identifies task-level timing and coordination as areas warranting further attention [7].
references.interpretation_limit: This supports the taxonomy and the review authors’ emphasis. It does not establish that no earlier study made our particular comparison. First publication was December 2025; the issue/volume is 2026.

references.supported_claim: Korivand et al. develop physiological task-load prediction and Q-learning-based adjustment, while explicitly reporting that their recorded wristband data could not be integrated directly for real-time use [8].
references.interpretation_limit: The limitation qualifies the implemented evidence. The framework should not be presented as a demonstrated end-to-end real-time wrist-triggered deployment.

references.manuscript_sections: 1. Introduction; 2.3. Physical tasks and participant experience
references.supported_claim: Recent work uses tangrams for collaborative HRI and as a simplified assembly task [15, 9]. SensCogAR uses tangrams as a proxy for small-object assembly, manipulating the visibility of piece contours to vary task demand [9].
references.interpretation_limit: Task rationale transfers at the level of spatial manipulation. Neither the validity of all nine current puzzles nor generalization to industrial assembly follows automatically. PDF p. 15 discusses task/context limitations.

references.supported_claim: Ojsteršek et al. personalize robot parameters using a preliminary skills test and analyze ECG recordings after the experiment [10].
references.interpretation_limit: Personalization and physiological measurement both occur, but the described ECG analysis is not the real-time control input. The PDF extraction repeats some layout text; locators refer to the actual PDF page.

references.supported_claim: Pereira et al.'s review documents heterogeneous workload measures and mixed cardiac findings across HRC studies [11].
references.interpretation_limit: We cite the review’s synthesis, not independently verified findings from every study it includes. It supplies no validation for our specific sensor, threshold or task.

references.version: arXiv v1; accepted HRI full paper
references.manuscript_sections: 1. Introduction; 2.3. Physical tasks and participant experience
references.supported_claim: Recent work uses tangrams for collaborative HRI and as a simplified assembly task [15, 9]. Tabatabaei et al. study gaze around robot failures during collaborative tangram solving [15].
references.interpretation_limit: This is a gaze-and-failure study, not a test of physiological or scheduled help. The local version is arXiv v1 of the accepted HRI paper, so its PDF page numbers differ from proceedings pagination.

references.version: Published version from university research-group website; journal issue 2018; online 2017
references.supported_claim: Earlier work by Teo et al. uses individualized physiological workload markers to trigger aid during robot supervision, imposing aid later when it has not been triggered [16].
references.interpretation_limit: The study uses personalized multimeasure workload logic in robot supervision. It does not establish our heart-rate-rise threshold or identical assistance mechanics. Online publication was 2017; journal issue 2018.

references.supported_claim: A recent HRI workshop proposal by Thunberg et al. emphasizes the practical, ethical, and methodological tensions of the wizard's role [17].
references.interpretation_limit: Supports identifying a methodological concern and research agenda. It is explicitly a workshop proposal, not completed empirical evidence or a validated operator protocol.

references.version: Author manuscript; published Human Factors 66(4), 1081–1102 (2024); first online 2022-11-11
references.supported_claim: Yang et al. compared workload-adaptive robotic suction with periodic support during surgical training [19]. Yang et al.'s surgical system uses EEG and eye tracking to inform adaptive suction, with a periodic comparator selected to approximate earlier observed assistance frequency [19].
references.interpretation_limit: This is the direct precedent that prevents a claim that the comparison itself is new. “Closest” is our assessment within the reviewed set, not proof from an exhaustive review. Online publication was 2022 despite the 2024 issue; the cached PDF is an author manuscript.

references.version: Published open-access committee report; university repository PDF
references.supported_claim: Cardiac measurement guidelines distinguish heart rate from beat-to-beat variability and emphasize signal quality and the influence of physical activity on wearable measurements [12] Wearable cardiac signals can be affected by movement and sensor contact [12]
references.interpretation_limit: Measurement guidance supports distinguishing HR from HRV and attending to artifacts. It does not validate this device, the three-minute baseline, the 15/60-second windows, the 5-bpm threshold, or inference of frustration from a flag.
references.manuscript_sections: 2.2. Physiological information in assistance; 6.2. Assistance timing and physiological feedback

references.supported_claim: GuideAI combines cardiac, gaze, and behavioral information to adapt learning content, pacing, and feedback [13]
references.interpretation_limit: A learning system combining multiple signals, not a robotic-assistance timing experiment. Its baseline/threshold text has inconsistencies and it uses interval-derived HRV; neither is imported as validation of our HR-rise detector. Its reported statistical method is not adopted.

references.version: arXiv v1 preprint; final journal venue not verified or asserted
references.supported_claim: In supply-chain operations, Smit et al. model collaborative human-robot order picking and jointly optimize picking efficiency and workload fairness through simulation [14] human-robot order-picking research examines efficiency alongside workload fairness [14]
references.interpretation_limit: Simulation of allocation policies, not a human experiment demonstrating tangram-to-supply-chain transfer. Workload fairness is distribution of picking burden, not NASA-TLX or physiological arousal.
references.manuscript_sections: 2.3. Physical tasks and participant experience; 6.3. Limitations and future work

references.version: Published Frontiers article, 18 June 2025; local filename names the corresponding author, first author is Wei
references.supported_claim: In a single-surgeon simulation study, Wei et al. identify subjective workload and mean heart rate among the influential features in a task-performance prediction model [18]
references.interpretation_limit: One expert surgeon and model-derived associations. Does not establish causation, population-wide prediction, assistance timing effectiveness, or validation of a heart-rate-rise trigger. SDHR is explicitly cautioned as an inadequate HRV proxy on p.5.

references.supported_claim: MRChaos uses tangrams to investigate robotic reasoning, planning, and manipulation from silhouette targets and extends its assembly approach to cutlery and soda-can arrangements [20] MRChaos demonstrates related spatial assembly tasks [20]
references.interpretation_limit: Autonomous robotic assembly with fixed piece sequence; not a human assistance-policy comparison. Cutlery/can experiments involve task-specific training with substituted objects, not unchanged tangram policy transfer, and no supply-chain user experiment.
references.manuscript_sections: 2.3. Physical tasks and participant experience; 6.3. Limitations and future work
